taxonomic_note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO; native to central and southwest Texas into northeastern Mexico.
look_here_first: Start with scale and the ligule. Lindheimer muhly is a large dense fountain-form bunchgrass, commonly around 1 m or more tall, with unusually long conspicuous membranous ligules and a tall feathery panicle. It dwarfs seep muhly and is completely unlike creeping nimblewill.

project_inclusion.range_basis: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Purola Preserve documents Muhlenbergia lindheimeri in the natural flora. Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed Williamson County treatment. Bell — Flora of North Central Texas documents M. lindheimeri from Bell County and notes its Edwards Plateau distribution.
project_inclusion.range_guardrail: Landscape-planted ornamental muhly is common; cultivated observations are not used as county-native proof.

best_field_traits: large perennial cespitose bunchgrass, often 100+ stems from the base
upright fountain-form habit, commonly around 1–1.4 m in regional material
narrow stiff blue-green to green blades, usually under about 4 mm wide
very conspicuous membranous ligule, roughly 10–39 mm in the Williamson treatment
tall erect terminal panicle, often 30–60+ cm long and becoming feathery
panicle branches densely flowered and ascending
short awn absent or only a few millimeters long
morphology_keys.comparison_training: Muhlenbergia reverchonii: Seep muhly is much smaller, usually 40–80 cm, with very fine involute blades, shorter ligules, and a more delicate airy reddish panicle. Muhlenbergia capillaris: Pink muhly is widely sold but is not a project-native Central Texas species. Do not identify ornamental pink-plumed muhly as M. lindheimeri by color alone. Muhlenbergia schreberi: Nimblewill is a low weak creeping perennial rooting at lower nodes; Lindheimer muhly is a robust upright basal bunchgrass.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Seep muhly is much smaller, usually 40–80 cm, with very fine involute blades, shorter ligules, and a more delicate airy reddish panicle. Pink muhly is widely sold but is not a project-native Central Texas species. Do not identify ornamental pink-plumed muhly as M. lindheimeri by color alone. Nimblewill is a low weak creeping perennial rooting at lower nodes; Lindheimer muhly is a robust upright basal bunchgrass.
